title: George Kelly: Personal Construct Theory
overview: George Kelly's personal construct theory is the textbook's representative of the cognitive approach. Kelly dropped the familiar concepts of the unconscious, drives, reinforcement and even motivation and emotion, and argued instead that people act like scientists: they form bipolar hypotheses, called constructs, to interpret and predict events, test them against experience and revise them. The theory is set out as a fundamental postulate and eleven corollaries. The chapter covers Kelly's life, his optimistic view of human nature, his assessment methods (the interview, the self-characterization sketch and the Role Construct Repertory Test), fixed role therapy, research including cognitive complexity and simplicity, and an evaluation of the theory.
objectives: Explain how Kelly's cognitive theory differs from other approaches and from the cognitive movement.
Describe Kelly's life and how his clinical experience shaped his theory.
Define construct, construct system and constructive alternativism, and explain the person-as-scientist model.
State the fundamental postulate and explain all eleven corollaries with examples.
Describe Kelly's position on questions about human nature.
Describe the interview, self-characterization sketch, REP Test and fixed role therapy.
Summarise research on constructs, cognitive complexity, cognitive simplicity and attributional complexity.
Evaluate the contributions and criticisms of Kelly's theory.

sections.heading: The Cognitive Movement in Psychology
sections.detailed:
Kelly's personal construct theory stands apart from every other approach in the textbook. Kelly himself cautioned readers that they would not find the familiar building blocks of personality psychology in his system: there is no unconscious, no ego, no needs or drives, no stimulus-response links, no reinforcement, and not even motivation or emotion as separate concepts. That raises an obvious puzzle: how can anyone explain personality without motivation and emotion?

Kelly's answer was that each person builds a set of cognitive constructs about the world. We interpret and organise the events and relationships of our lives into a system or pattern. From that pattern we make predictions about ourselves, other people and events, and those predictions shape how we respond and act. So the route to understanding a personality is to understand the person's patterns, the particular ways he or she organises, or construes, the world. A central claim follows: how we interpret an event matters more than the event itself.

The margin definition sums up personal construct theory as Kelly's account of personality in terms of cognitive processes. We are able to interpret behaviour and events, and we use that understanding both to steer our own behaviour and to predict what other people will do.

Opposition to behaviourism and psychoanalysis. Like Maslow, Kelly rejected both the behavioural and the psychoanalytic approaches, because both deny that people can take charge of their own lives, make their own decisions and follow a course they have chosen. In his view, behaviourism treats people as passive responders to environmental stimuli, while psychoanalysis treats them as passive responders to unconscious forces. For Kelly, by contrast, people are a form of motion that propels itself; nothing outside us does the pushing (the chapter cites Fransella and Neimeyer, 2003, on this point).

This opening sets up the whole chapter: personality is about active, conscious interpretation and prediction, not about hidden forces or conditioned responses.
sections.simple: Kelly's theory leaves out the usual ideas like the unconscious, drives, reinforcement, even motivation and emotion. Instead, he said each of us builds mental patterns (constructs) to interpret events and predict what will happen. How we interpret an event matters more than the event itself, and we are active agents, not passive responders.
keyPoints: Kelly's system omits the unconscious, ego, needs, drives, S-R, reinforcement, motivation and emotion
People build cognitive constructs to interpret events and predict the future
Our interpretation of events matters more than the events themselves
Like Maslow, Kelly opposed behaviourism and psychoanalysis for making people passive
For Kelly, people propel themselves; nothing does it to us

sections.heading: An Experiential-Based Theory; Are Psychologists Superior Beings?
sections.detailed:
Theory built from clinical experience. Kelly's theory grew out of his work as a clinician, but he read that clinical experience very differently from Freud and the other therapist-theorists. The model of human nature he arrived at is unusual: people operate the way scientists do.

The scientist model. Scientists build theories and hypotheses and test them against reality through experiments. If results support a theory, it is kept; if not, it is dropped or revised and tested again. Personality psychologists themselves work this way. Yet Kelly noticed a double standard: psychologists do not grant their research subjects the same intellectual and rational abilities they claim for themselves. It is as though psychology holds two theories of human nature, one for scientists and another for everyone else.

The logical implication of that double standard is that psychologists treat their subjects as incapable of rational functioning, as driven by conflicting drives or as victims of unconscious forces. People are assumed to function mainly at an emotional level and to rarely use cognition to learn, think, weigh experience or solve problems, which is plainly not how psychologists picture their own functioning.

Are psychologists superior beings? Kelly's answer was no. Psychologists are no different from the people they study: whatever explains one explains the other. Both are concerned with predicting and controlling the events in their lives, and both can do so rationally.

Personal constructs as personal theories. Just as scientists build theories, every one of us builds theories, which Kelly called personal constructs, to predict and control what happens to us. The way to understand someone's personality, therefore, is to examine his or her personal constructs. This "person as scientist" idea is the heart of the theory and the answer to the review question about what Kelly meant by saying we all function like scientists.
sections.simple: Kelly built his theory from his clinical work and concluded that ordinary people act like scientists: they form hypotheses, test them and revise them. He criticised psychologists for treating themselves as rational but their subjects as irrational. Everyone builds personal constructs to predict and control life, so studying those constructs is how we understand personality.
keyPoints: Theory derived from Kelly's clinical experience
People function like scientists: hypothesise, test, keep or revise
Psychologists wrongly hold one theory for themselves and another for their subjects
Psychologists are not superior beings; both groups predict and control events rationally
Our personal theories are personal constructs; studying them reveals personality

sections.heading: Kelly and the Cognitive Movement
sections.detailed:
The cognitive movement began around 1960 and now dominates mainstream experimental psychology. Despite the shared word "cognitive," that movement has not taken up Kelly's work, because his theory does not match its subject matter or methods.

Key differences. Kelly worked as a clinician concerned with the conscious constructs by which people organise their lives. Cognitive psychologists, in contrast, study both cognitive variables and overt behaviour, and they do so mainly in experimental rather than clinical settings. They also do not restrict themselves to personality: they study overt behaviour and learning in social situations, and they hold that cognitive processes such as learning shape how a person responds to a given stimulus situation.

Little influence. Although cognitive psychology took hold after Kelly published his theory, his work had little impact on it. At most, Kelly can be seen as a precursor of contemporary cognitive psychology. The two share the label cognitive, with its interest in conscious mental activity, but little else.

Placing Kelly in perspective. Kelly deserves credit for recognising the importance of cognitive processes, but this has to be kept in proportion. His theory is not part of mainstream American psychology as experimental psychologists define it. That, however, does not reduce its usefulness for the study of personality.

For exams, this section answers the review question on the relationship between Kelly's theory and modern cognitive psychology: shared terminology and an interest in conscious processes, but different settings (clinical vs experimental), different focus (personality vs broader behaviour and learning), and little direct influence.
sections.simple: The cognitive movement that started around 1960 did not adopt Kelly's ideas. Kelly was a clinician focused on conscious constructs, while cognitive psychologists run experiments on cognition and overt behaviour beyond personality. Kelly is at best a forerunner; the two share the word cognitive but little else.
keyPoints: Cognitive movement began c. 1960 and dominates experimental psychology
It did not embrace Kelly: different subject matter and methods
Kelly: clinical, conscious constructs; cognitive psychology: experimental, cognition plus overt behaviour
Kelly is at best a precursor; shares the term cognitive but little else
Not mainstream, yet still useful for studying personality

sections.heading: The Life of Kelly (1905-1967): Childhood, An Erratic Education, No Interest in Psychology
sections.detailed:
Childhood. Kelly was born on a Kansas farm, an only child who received much attention and affection from his parents. They were religious fundamentalists committed to helping the less fortunate, and they opposed frivolous amusements such as dancing and card playing. When he was 4, the family travelled by covered wagon to Colorado to try farming there but soon returned to Kansas.

An erratic education. His early schooling was irregular and came as much from his parents as from teachers. At 13 he went to high school in Wichita and rarely lived at home afterwards. In 1926 he earned a bachelor's degree in physics and mathematics from Park College in Parkville, Missouri, but by then his interests had moved from science to social problems, and his future was unclear.

A wandering early career. He worked briefly as an engineer, then taught at a labour college in Minneapolis. He next became a speech instructor for the American Banking Association and taught citizenship classes to immigrants. He then earned a master's degree in educational sociology from the University of Kansas in Lawrence, and took a job at a junior college in Iowa, teaching various courses and coaching drama.

No interest in psychology. Nothing in this path pointed to psychology. His college psychology coursework left him unimpressed. In his first course he sat at the back of a large class and perked up only when the professor wrote S, an arrow and R on the board, hoping the real substance was finally coming. After a few more classes he gave up, because he could not work out what the arrow between stimulus and response stood for, and he says he never did. So the behaviourist, experimental approach failed to engage him. He also tried psychoanalysis, with no better result: reading a book by Freud, he felt growing disbelief that anyone could write, let alone publish, such "nonsense" (his word).

Relevance. These early rejections of both S-R behaviourism and Freud foreshadow the theory's refusal to use stimuli, responses, reinforcement or the unconscious.
sections.simple: Kelly grew up an only child on a Kansas farm with strict religious parents. His education was patchy; he took a physics and maths degree, then drifted through engineering, teaching and a master's in educational sociology. Psychology bored him at first: he could not see what the S-R arrow meant and found Freud unbelievable.
keyPoints: Born 1905 on a Kansas farm; only child of fundamentalist parents
Erratic schooling; B.A. physics and mathematics, Park College, 1926
Varied jobs: engineer, labour college, speech instructor, citizenship teacher, drama coach
M.A. in educational sociology, University of Kansas
Unimpressed by S-R behaviourism (the arrow) and by Freud's writing

sections.heading: The Life of Kelly: Finding Himself and Psychology, An Intellectual Approach to Counseling, Becoming a Major Force
sections.detailed:
Finding psychology. In 1929 Kelly won a fellowship to the University of Edinburgh, Scotland. During that year he earned a Bachelor of Education degree and at last developed an interest in psychology. Back in the United States he did doctoral work at the State University of Iowa and received his Ph.D. in 1931.

Switching to clinical work. He started his academic career at Fort Hays Kansas State College during the economic depression of the 1930s. There was no money for research in physiological psychology, the area he had trained in, so he moved into clinical psychology, where there was a need. He set up a clinical service for the local public schools and for his college's students, and ran travelling clinics that went from school to school. This exposed him to many kinds of problems and let him experiment with different treatment approaches.

An open, self-taught therapist. Kelly was not tied to any one therapeutic technique or personality theory. He freely used traditional assessment and treatment methods as well as his own. He largely taught himself therapy by assuming each new client was as much a scientist as he was (Routh, 2011).

How his clients shaped the theory. His clinical experience strongly influenced personal construct theory. His clients were not severely disturbed psychotics in hospitals or neurotics with heavy emotional problems; they were students referred by their teachers for counselling. Compared with psychiatric or psychoanalytic patients, they could discuss their concerns rationally and express problems in intellectual terms, the level expected in an academic setting. The analytical, logical attitude of the classroom carried over into counselling. The chapter suggests that had Kelly spent his formative years with schizophrenic patients in an institution, his theory might not have leaned so heavily on cognitive, information-processing abilities. This is the answer to the review question about how his clients influenced his theory.

Becoming a major force. During World War II he served in the U.S. Navy as a psychologist in the Bureau of Medicine and Surgery in Washington DC. After the war ended in 1945 he taught for a year at the University of Maryland, then joined Ohio State University, replacing Carl Rogers. He spent 19 years there teaching, refining the theory and doing research, and lectured worldwide on how personal construct theory could help resolve international tensions. In 1965 he accepted Abraham Maslow's invitation to an endowed chair at Brandeis University but died soon after (1967). He was a major force in the growth of clinical psychology after World War II, serving as president of the Clinical and Consulting divisions of the American Psychological Association and of the American Board of Examiners in Professional Psychology.
sections.simple: Kelly found psychology during a year at Edinburgh and got his Ph.D. from Iowa in 1931. During the Depression he switched from physiological to clinical psychology and counselled school and college students, who could talk about problems rationally, which shaped his very cognitive theory. Later at Ohio State (replacing Carl Rogers) he became a leader of clinical psychology.
keyPoints: 1929 Edinburgh fellowship: B.Ed. and first real interest in psychology; Ph.D. Iowa 1931
Depression-era shift from physiological to clinical psychology at Fort Hays; travelling school clinics
Self-taught therapist who treated each client as a fellow scientist
Rational student clients made the theory heavily cognitive
Navy psychologist in WWII; 19 years at Ohio State replacing Carl Rogers; Brandeis chair via Maslow; died 1967
President of APA Clinical and Consulting divisions and the American Board of Examiners in Professional Psychology

sections.heading: Personal Construct Theory; Life Is a Construct
sections.detailed:
People as scientists of everyday life. Kelly proposed that we perceive and organise experience the way scientists do: we form hypotheses about the environment and test them against daily reality. We observe the facts of our experience and interpret them in our own way. This personal interpreting or construing of experience is our unique view of events (Winter and Proctor, 2014), the pattern into which we fit them. Kelly described these patterns as transparent templates laid over the realities of the world.

The sunglasses analogy. The patterns can be compared to tinted sunglasses. One person's lenses are bluish, another's greenish, so several people looking at the same scene see it differently. In the same way, the patterns we build to make sense of the world colour what we perceive. This unique pattern created by each individual is what Kelly called the construct system.

What a construct is. A construct is a person's unique way of looking at life: an intellectual hypothesis devised to explain or interpret events. The margin definition adds that constructs are bipolar or dichotomous, such as tall versus short or honest versus dishonest. We behave on the expectation that our constructs will predict and explain reality, and, like scientists, we keep testing them: we act on our constructs and then evaluate the results.

The student-and-professor example. A student about to fail an introductory psychology course watches the professor all semester and decides that the professor is superior, authoritarian and self-important. The student forms the hypothesis (construct) that feeding the professor's inflated self-image will win a favourable response, and tests it by reading an article the professor wrote and praising it. If the flattered professor gives a good grade, the construct is confirmed and can be reused with that professor or similar ones. If the student still fails, the construct has proved inappropriate and a new one is needed for that professor.

This illustrates the full cycle: observe, form a construct, act on it, check the outcome, then keep or replace the construct. It answers the review question on Kelly's definition of a construct.
sections.simple: We see the world through our own personal patterns, like tinted sunglasses, so different people see the same scene differently. A construct is a personal hypothesis used to interpret and predict events, always two-sided (like honest versus dishonest). We act on our constructs, check the results and keep or drop them, like a scientist testing a theory.
keyPoints: We construe experience like scientists: form hypotheses and test them against daily life
Patterns act like tinted sunglasses; the individual's total pattern is the construct system
A construct is an intellectual hypothesis used to interpret or explain events
Constructs are bipolar (tall vs short, honest vs dishonest)
Student-professor example: confirmed constructs are kept, failed ones replaced

sections.heading: Constructive Alternativism: Adapting to the World
sections.detailed:
Building an inventory of constructs. Across our lives we develop a great many constructs, one for nearly every type of person or situation we meet. Our inventory grows as we encounter new people and situations, and we periodically alter or discard constructs as circumstances change. Revising constructs is a necessary and continuous process: we must always have an alternative construct available to apply to a situation.

Why flexibility is essential. If constructs were rigid and could not be revised, which is what would happen if personality were completely fixed by childhood influences, we would be unable to cope with new situations. Kelly's name for this adaptability is constructive alternativism. It expresses the view that we are not controlled by our constructs; we are free to revise them or swap them for alternatives.

Significance. Constructive alternativism is the philosophical basis of Kelly's optimism and his belief in free will. It directly contrasts with deterministic theories such as Freud's, in which early childhood sets personality in place. Because there are always alternative ways to construe any event, people are never trapped by their present interpretation; change is always possible. This idea also underlies Kelly's therapy, since fixed role therapy works by helping clients try out alternative constructs.

For exam answers on why Kelly believed we must always revise our constructs (a review question), stress three points: the world and our circumstances keep changing; constructs are tested hypotheses that can fail; and without alternatives we would be unable to cope with anything new, as if determined by childhood.
sections.simple: We build many constructs over life and keep changing or replacing them as situations change. Kelly called this freedom to revise or swap constructs constructive alternativism. If our constructs could never change, as they would if childhood fixed our personality, we could not cope with anything new.
keyPoints: We develop constructs for almost every person and situation, and the inventory keeps growing
Constructs are altered or discarded as situations change; revision is continuous
Rigid constructs (as if fixed by childhood) would leave us unable to cope
Constructive alternativism: we are free to revise or replace constructs with alternatives
Basis of Kelly's anti-determinism and of fixed role therapy

sections.heading: Ways of Anticipating Life Events: The Fundamental Postulate
sections.detailed:
Scientific format. Kelly presented personal construct theory in the format of a scientific theory: one fundamental postulate followed by 11 corollaries (summarised in Table 11.1 of the chapter).

The fundamental postulate. It states that our psychological processes are directed by the ways in which we anticipate events. Two words carry the meaning.

"Processes." By choosing this word, Kelly signalled that personality is a continually flowing, moving process rather than a fixed structure. Our psychological processes are directed by our constructs, that is, by how each of us construes the world.

"Anticipate." Kelly's constructs are anticipatory. We use them to predict the future, so that we have some idea of the consequences of our actions and of what is likely to happen if we behave in a certain way.

The eleven corollaries in brief (Table 11.1):
Construction: because repeated events are similar, we can anticipate how we will experience such events in future.
Individuality: people perceive events in different ways.
Organization: we arrange constructs in patterns according to their similarities and differences.
Dichotomy: constructs are bipolar; an idea of honesty must include dishonesty.
Choice: we pick the alternative of each construct that works best for us, the one that lets us predict outcomes.
Range: constructs may apply to many people or situations or be limited to one.
Experience: we continually test constructs against experience to make sure they remain useful.
Modulation: we may modify constructs in light of new experiences.
Fragmentation: we may hold contradictory or inconsistent subordinate constructs within the overall system.
Commonality: although constructs are unique, people in compatible groups or cultures may hold similar constructs.
Sociality: we try to understand how others think and predict what they will do, and adjust our behaviour accordingly.

Linking point. The postulate explains why anticipation shapes personality (a review question): since our processes are directed by how we anticipate events and other people, our constructs, choices and roles all flow from those anticipations.
sections.simple: Kelly organised his theory like a science: one fundamental postulate and 11 corollaries. The postulate says our psychological processes are directed by how we anticipate events. Personality is an ongoing process, and constructs exist to predict what will happen next.
keyPoints: Theory = 1 fundamental postulate + 11 corollaries (Table 11.1)
Postulate: psychological processes are directed by the ways we anticipate events
'Processes' means personality is continually flowing, not static
'Anticipate' means constructs are used to predict consequences of our actions
Corollaries: construction, individuality, organization, dichotomy, choice, range, experience, modulation, fragmentation, commonality, sociality

sections.heading: The Construction Corollary
sections.detailed:
Similarities among repeated events. Kelly believed that no event can be experienced exactly as it was the first time. An event can recur, but the experience will differ. Rewatching a film you saw last month, for instance, may feel different: your mood may have changed, and events in the intervening month may have affected your attitudes and emotions, such as reading something unpleasant about one of the actors or feeling happier because your grades are improving.

Recurring themes. Even though repeated events are not experienced identically, recurrent features or themes emerge; some aspects of a situation resemble what we met before. On the basis of these similarities we can anticipate how we will deal with that type of event in future. Our predictions rest on the assumption that future events, while not exact copies of past ones, will nonetheless be similar.

Example. Some scenes in the film probably affect you the same way every time. If you enjoyed the car chases first time, you will likely enjoy them again; you base your behaviour (choosing to rewatch) on that anticipation. Past themes reappear in the future, and we formulate our constructs from these recurring themes.

Exam angle. The review question on what influences how we anticipate events similar to past events is answered here: our current mood and intervening experiences make each repetition different, but the recurring similarities allow prediction.
sections.simple: No event is ever experienced exactly the same way twice, because our mood and circumstances change. But repeated events share common themes, and those similarities let us predict how we will experience similar events in future. Constructs are built from these recurring themes.
keyPoints: No event is experienced exactly the same way twice
Mood and intervening experiences change how a repeated event feels
Recurring themes or similarities still emerge
We anticipate future events on the basis of these similarities
Constructs are formulated from recurring themes (film car-chase example)

sections.heading: The Individuality Corollary
sections.detailed:
Individual differences in interpreting events. With this corollary Kelly brought individual differences into his theory. People differ in how they perceive or interpret any given event, and because they construe events differently, they form different constructs.

Constructs as interpretations, not copies. Our constructs reflect less the objective reality of an event than the unique interpretation each of us places on it. Two people at the same lecture, match or family function may come away with entirely different constructs because they read the situation differently. This links directly to the sunglasses analogy: each person's lenses tint the same scene in a different way.

Contrast with the organization corollary (a review question). The individuality corollary concerns differences in the constructs themselves: people form different constructs because they interpret events differently. The organization corollary adds that even people who hold similar constructs can still differ, because they arrange those constructs into different patterns or hierarchies. So individuality is about what constructs we have; organization is about how we structure them.

Link to uniqueness. Together with the commonality corollary, this corollary defines Kelly's moderate position on uniqueness versus universality: individuality stresses that many of our constructs, and so our selves, are unique.
sections.simple: People interpret the same event in different ways, so they form different constructs. Our constructs reflect our own interpretation more than objective reality. This is where Kelly explains individual differences.
keyPoints: Introduces individual differences into the theory
People perceive and interpret the same event differently
Different interpretations produce different constructs
Constructs reflect personal interpretation more than objective reality
Differs from organization corollary: content of constructs vs their arrangement

sections.heading: The Organization Corollary
sections.detailed:
Relationships among constructs. We organise individual constructs into a pattern based on how we see their interrelationships, their similarities and differences. People with similar constructs may still differ from one another if they organise those constructs into different patterns.

Hierarchy. Typically constructs are arranged in a hierarchy, with some subordinate to others, and a construct can include one or more subordinate constructs. For example, the construct good might include the subordinates intelligent and moral. So when we meet someone who fits our idea of a good person, we expect him or her also to be intelligent and to have high moral standards.

Stability and change. The relationships among constructs usually last longer than the specific constructs, but they too can change. A person who feels insulted by someone who seems more intelligent might move intelligent from beneath good to beneath bad.

Predictive efficiency. The only valid test of a construct system is its predictive efficiency. If the way our constructs are organised no longer helps us predict events usefully, we modify it.

Exam angle. When asked how individuality differs from organization (review question), note that individuality explains differences in the constructs people form, while organization explains how even similar constructs can yield different personalities because of the way they are structured into hierarchies.
sections.simple: We arrange our constructs into patterns, usually hierarchies where broader constructs contain narrower ones (good includes intelligent and moral). Two people with the same constructs can still differ if they organise them differently. If the organisation stops predicting well, we change it.
keyPoints: Constructs are organised by perceived similarities and differences
Usually hierarchical: superordinate constructs contain subordinate ones
Example: good includes intelligent and moral
Relationships are more enduring than individual constructs but can change (intelligent moved under bad)
The only valid test of a construct system is predictive efficiency

sections.heading: The Dichotomy Corollary
sections.detailed:
Two mutually exclusive alternatives. All constructs are bipolar, or dichotomous. Kelly saw this as necessary for correctly anticipating future events. Just as we notice similarities among people or events, we must also account for differences.

The honesty example. It is not enough to have a construct describing a friend as honest; we must also have the opposite, dishonesty, to explain how an honest person differs from one who is not. If we made no such distinction and assumed everyone was honest, a construct about honesty would help us predict nothing about people we will meet. Someone can be expected to be honest only in contrast to someone expected to be dishonest. So the correct construct is honest versus dishonest. Constructs must always be framed as a pair of mutually exclusive alternatives.

Why constructs must be dichotomous (review question). A construct is a tool for prediction, and prediction requires discrimination. A pole without its opposite would apply to everything and therefore distinguish nothing.

Connections. This corollary sets up the choice corollary (we must choose between the two poles) and underlies the Role Construct Repertory Test, which assumes people construe events in terms of like versus unlike, with an emergent pole and an implicit pole.
sections.simple: Every construct has two opposite ends, like honest versus dishonest. We need the opposite pole to make any distinction; if everyone were honest, the idea of honesty would predict nothing. So constructs are always pairs of mutually exclusive alternatives.
keyPoints: All constructs are bipolar (dichotomous)
We must account for differences as well as similarities
Honest only makes sense in contrast to dishonest
Without the opposite pole, a construct cannot predict anything
Basis for the choice corollary and the REP Test

sections.heading: The Choice Corollary
sections.detailed:
Freedom of choice. Freedom of choice runs throughout Kelly's writings. Because each construct has two opposing poles (dichotomy corollary), in every situation we must choose the alternative that works best for us, the one that lets us anticipate or predict the outcome of future events.

Security versus adventure. Kelly said we have some latitude in choosing, and he framed it as a choice between security and adventure. Imagine choosing between two courses. One is easy, similar to a course you have already taken, and taught by a professor known for high grades with little work. There is almost no risk, but little reward either; the professor is dull and you have already covered much of the material. It is the secure choice because you can predict the consequences very accurately. The other course is a gamble: a new professor said to be tough, an unfamiliar subject, but one you are curious about. You cannot predict the outcome accurately; risk is higher, but so are potential reward and satisfaction.

Low risk versus high risk. The secure option is low risk, low reward and has high predictive efficiency; the adventurous one is high risk, high reward and has lower predictive efficiency. Kelly believed we face such choices all our lives: choices between defining and extending the construct system. The secure choice repeats past experiences and so further defines and limits the system; the adventurous choice extends it by taking in new experiences and events.

Explaining unrewarding behaviour. The common tendency to choose the secure option may explain why people persist in unrewarding behaviour. Why do some people keep acting aggressively even when constantly rebuffed? Kelly's answer: aggression is their low-risk choice because they know what reactions to expect. They do not know how people will respond to friendliness because they have rarely tried it; friendliness might bring greater rewards, but also greater uncertainty.

Key principle. Our choices are made on the basis of how well they let us anticipate events, not necessarily on what is best for us. In the best scientific tradition, each of us wants to predict the future with the greatest possible certainty. (Reflections later notes that Kelly never explained what decides whether a person opts for security or adventure.)
sections.simple: Since every construct has two poles, we have to choose one, and we pick the one that best helps us predict what will happen. Often this is a choice between a safe, predictable option (security) and a risky, rewarding one (adventure). People often stick with the safe option, even unrewarding behaviour like aggression, because it is predictable.
keyPoints: We choose the pole of a construct that best helps us predict outcomes
Choice framed as security vs adventure
Secure = low risk, low reward, high predictive efficiency; defines and limits the construct system
Adventurous = high risk, high reward, lower predictive efficiency; extends the construct system
Explains persistent aggression: it is the predictable, low-risk choice
Choices aim at prediction, not necessarily at what is best for us

sections.heading: The Range Corollary
sections.detailed:
The range of convenience. Few personal constructs are relevant to every situation. The construct tall versus short, for example, has a limited range of convenience or applicability: it is useful for buildings, trees or basketball players but useless for describing a pizza or the weather.

Broad and narrow constructs. Some constructs can be applied to many situations or people; others are limited to perhaps one person or situation. The range of convenience is the spectrum of events to which a construct can be applied (margin definition).

A matter of personal choice. How wide a construct's range is depends on the individual. We might apply loyal versus disloyal to everyone we meet, or only to family members, or only to our pet dog.

What is excluded matters too. According to Kelly, to understand personality fully it is just as important to know what lies outside a construct's range of convenience as what lies inside it.

Exam angle. Review questions ask what the range of convenience is and invite you to reflect on the range of your own construct such as cheerful versus sad (for example, whether you apply it to people only, or also to music, weather or places). The mechanism Kelly proposed for changes in range is permeability, covered under the modulation corollary.
sections.simple: Each construct applies only to certain things; this is its range of convenience. Tall versus short works for trees and people but not for pizza or weather. How widely we apply a construct is personal, and knowing what a construct excludes is as important as what it includes.
keyPoints: Range of convenience = spectrum of events a construct can be applied to
Tall vs short fits buildings and basketball players, not pizza or weather
Some constructs are broad, others limited to one person or situation
Range is a matter of personal choice (loyal vs disloyal example)
Knowing what a construct excludes is as important as what it includes

sections.heading: The Experience Corollary
sections.detailed:
Exposure to new experiences. Each construct is a hypothesis generated from past experience to predict future events, and each is tested against reality by checking how well it predicts a given event. Because most of us meet new experiences every day, testing the fit of our constructs is an ongoing process. If a construct does not validly predict the outcome of a situation, it must be reformulated or replaced.

Constructs change with life. We therefore evaluate and reinterpret our constructs as our environment changes. Constructs that served us at 16 may be useless or even harmful at 40, because experiences in between will have led us to revise the construct system. If someone never had new experiences, the construct system would never need to change; but for most people life means meeting new people and facing new challenges, so we must keep re-construing our experiences and constructs.

Significance. This corollary supports constructive alternativism and the answer to the review question on why we must always revise our constructs. It also expresses the scientific cycle at the core of the theory: predict, test against experience, revise.
sections.simple: We keep testing our constructs against new experiences every day. If a construct predicts badly, we change or replace it. Constructs that worked at 16 might be useless at 40, because life keeps bringing new people and challenges.
keyPoints: Constructs are hypotheses tested against each new experience
Testing is continuous because new experiences occur daily
Poor predictors must be reformulated or replaced
Constructs useful at 16 may be useless or harmful at 40
Without new experiences, the construct system would never need to change

sections.heading: The Modulation Corollary
sections.detailed:
Adapting to new experiences. Constructs differ in their permeability. To permeate means to penetrate or pass through. A permeable construct lets new elements enter its range of convenience; it is open to new events and experiences and can be revised or extended by them. The margin definition puts it simply: permeability is the idea that constructs can be revised and extended in light of new experiences.

Degree of modulation. How far our construct system can be modulated, or adjusted, by new experience and learning depends on how permeable the individual constructs are. An impermeable or rigid construct cannot be changed whatever our experiences tell us.

The prejudice example. A bigoted person may apply the construct high intelligence versus low intelligence in a fixed, impermeable way to members of a certain ethnic minority, believing all of them to have low intelligence. New experiences will not penetrate or change this belief: no matter how many highly intelligent members of that group the person meets, the construct stays the same. It becomes a barrier to learning and to new ideas.

Exam angle. The review question asking what mechanism Kelly proposed to explain changes in a construct's range of convenience is answered by permeability. Permeable constructs can widen or alter their range as new elements are admitted; impermeable ones cannot.
sections.simple: Some constructs are open to change (permeable) and some are rigid (impermeable). Permeable constructs let new experiences in and get revised or extended. A prejudiced belief is an example of an impermeable construct that no amount of contrary evidence changes.
keyPoints: Permeability = capacity of a construct to be revised and extended by new experiences
Permeable constructs admit new elements into their range of convenience
How much the system can be modulated depends on permeability
Impermeable (rigid) constructs cannot change regardless of experience
Prejudice example: impermeable constructs block learning
Permeability is the mechanism for changes in range of convenience

sections.heading: The Fragmentation Corollary
sections.detailed:
Competition among constructs. Kelly believed some constructs within a system can be incompatible even though they coexist within the overall pattern. Our construct system changes as we evaluate new experiences, but new constructs do not necessarily derive from old ones. A new construct may fit an old one in one situation but become inconsistent with it when the situation changes.

The friend-enemy example. A man meets a woman in a psychology class and is attracted to her. She is also a psychology major with interests like his, so she fits the friend pole of his construct friend versus enemy, someone to like and respect. The next day he sees her at a political rally loudly voicing conservative views opposite to his own liberal opinions. Now she also fits the opposite pole: in that situation she has become the enemy.

How we tolerate inconsistency. This inconsistency lies at a subordinate level of his construct system: in one situation she is a friend, in another an enemy. His broader, superordinate construct, that liberals are friends and conservatives are enemies, is left undisturbed. According to Kelly, this is how we tolerate subordinate inconsistencies without damaging the overall construct system. (A photo caption in the chapter makes the same point: people may be friends over a board game but adversaries in a political debate.)

Exam angle. The review question on how it is possible to hold incompatible constructs is answered here: the contradictions are confined to subordinate constructs tied to particular situations, while the superordinate structure remains consistent.
sections.simple: We can hold contradictory constructs at the same time, as long as the contradiction stays at a lower, situation-specific level. A man may see a woman as a friend in class and an enemy at a political rally, while his broader belief (liberals are friends, conservatives enemies) stays intact.
keyPoints: Incompatible constructs can coexist within the system
New constructs do not necessarily derive from old ones
Constructs consistent in one situation may clash in another
Friend-vs-enemy example: classmate becomes enemy at a political rally
Inconsistency is tolerated at the subordinate level; superordinate constructs stay intact

sections.heading: The Commonality Corollary
sections.detailed:
Similarities among people in interpreting events. Because people construe events differently, each develops unique constructs. Yet people also show similarities in how they construe events. Kelly proposed that if several people construe an experience in a similar way, we can conclude that their cognitive processes are similar.

Culture and shared constructs. A group of people sharing the same cultural norms and ideals will have much in common in their anticipations and expectations of one another, and will construe many experiences the same way. People from the same culture may therefore resemble one another in behaviour and characteristics even though each has been exposed to different individual life events.

Balancing individuality. This corollary counterbalances the individuality corollary. Together they give Kelly's moderate position on uniqueness versus universality: many constructs are unique, but people in compatible groups or cultures hold similar ones.

Limits. As the next corollary explains, merely construing events the same way does not by itself produce good social relationships; that requires construing the other person's constructs.
sections.simple: Even though each person's constructs are unique, people from the same culture often interpret events in similar ways. When people construe an experience similarly, their thinking processes are similar. That is why people from one culture can behave alike despite different life events.
keyPoints: People show similarities as well as differences in construing events
Similar construing implies similar cognitive processes
Shared cultural norms produce shared anticipations and expectations
People of the same culture may resemble each other despite different life events
Balances the individuality corollary: Kelly's moderate stance on uniqueness

sections.heading: The Sociality Corollary
sections.detailed:
Interpersonal relationships. People in the same culture tend to construe events similarly, but this alone does not create positive social relationships. It is not enough for one person to construe experiences in the same way as another. The first person must also construe the other person's constructs; we must understand how another person thinks in order to anticipate how that person will predict events.

Everyday example: driving. We construe other people's constructs routinely. On the road we stake our lives on anticipating what other drivers will do, expecting them to stop at red lights and move on green. Only when we can predict with some certainty what drivers, friends, bosses or teachers will do can we adjust our behaviour to theirs, and while we adapt to them, they adapt to us.

Roles. Each person takes on a role with respect to others: one with a partner, another with a child, another with a supervisor at work. Each role is a pattern of behaviour that develops from understanding how the other person construes events. In this sense we fit ourselves into the other person's constructs.

Exam angle. The review question on why it is important to construe other people's constructs is answered here: it lets us predict others' behaviour, coordinate with them (as in traffic), form workable relationships and play appropriate roles. This idea also reappears in the Roy Taylor fixed role sketch, which stresses seeing the world through other people's eyes.
sections.simple: To get along with people, we need to understand how they think (construe their constructs), not just think like them. This lets us predict others, as when we trust drivers to stop at red lights. Our roles with partners, children and bosses come from understanding how each of them sees things.
keyPoints: Similar construing alone does not produce good relationships
We must construe other people's constructs to predict their behaviour
Driving example: we predict other drivers and adjust; they adjust to us
Roles are behaviour patterns built from understanding others' construing
We fit ourselves into other people's constructs

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Optimistic image. Kelly's theory presents an optimistic, even flattering, picture of human nature (Kelly, 1969). He treated people as rational beings able to build a framework of constructs through which to view the world. We are the authors, not the victims, of our destiny.

Free will versus determinism. Kelly's view grants us free will: the ability to choose the direction of our lives, and to change when necessary by revising old constructs and forming new ones. We are not committed to a path set in childhood or adolescence. He rejected determinism and did not regard past events as determining present behaviour. We are not prisoners of toilet training, early sexual experiences or parental rejection, nor bound by biological instincts or unconscious forces.

Nature of motivation. We need no push from internal drives or needs, because we are motivated simply by the fact of being alive; Kelly saw no reason for any further explanation.

Nature versus nurture. Kelly did not discuss heredity, but he held that we are not wholly determined by environment either. We live by constructs based on our interpretation of events, so it is our rational mental processes, not the specific events, that shape personality.

Ultimate goal. Kelly did not propose a necessary life goal, but one can infer that our goal is to establish a construct system that enables us to predict events.

Past versus future. Our orientation is clearly toward the future, since constructs are formulated to anticipate events.

Uniqueness versus universality. Kelly took a moderate position: the commonality corollary says people in the same culture develop similar constructs, while the individuality corollary stresses the uniqueness of many constructs and thus of the self.

Summary table for exams: free will (yes), determinism (rejected), future-oriented, environment not fully determining and heredity not discussed, moderate on uniqueness, optimistic, goal inferred as predictive construct system.
sections.simple: Kelly saw people as rational and free, the authors of their own destiny, not prisoners of childhood, instincts or the unconscious. We are motivated just by being alive and face the future, aiming to build constructs that predict events. On uniqueness he took a middle position.
keyPoints: Optimistic image: rational beings who author their own destiny
Free will; determinism rejected; not prisoners of childhood or instincts
Motivation: simply being alive; no drives or needs required
Future-oriented; inferred goal is a construct system that predicts events
Heredity not discussed; environment not fully determining; interpretation matters
Moderate on uniqueness vs universality (commonality vs individuality)

sections.heading: Assessment in Kelly's Theory: The Interview and Self-Characterization Sketches
sections.detailed:
The interview. Kelly's main assessment method was the interview. His famous advice was that if you do not know what is going on in someone's mind, you should ask, because the person may tell you (1958). He adopted what he called a "credulous attitude," accepting the client's words at face value, since he believed this was the best way to discover the person's constructs. He recognised that a client might deliberately lie or distort events, but held that what the client said must be respected even if not always fully believed.

Self-characterization sketches. A second technique for assessing a construct system is to have the person write a self-characterization sketch. Kelly instructed clients to write a character sketch of themselves, using their own name, as though they were the main character in a play, written by a friend who knew them very intimately and sympathetically, perhaps better than anyone actually could (1955). The margin definition describes the sketch as a technique for assessing a construct system, specifically how a person perceives himself or herself in relation to other people. Kelly found it useful for exactly that purpose.

Use in therapy (review question). Besides revealing self-perceptions, the self-characterization sketch is the starting point of fixed role therapy: the therapist compares the client's negative self-perceptions in the sketch with a new fixed role sketch built from different constructs.

Why these methods suit the theory. Because Kelly saw people as rational scientists who are consciously aware of their constructs, he trusted them to report those constructs directly, unlike psychoanalysts who look for hidden unconscious meaning.
sections.simple: Kelly mainly assessed people by simply asking them, taking their answers at face value (the credulous attitude). He also had clients write a self-characterization sketch, describing themselves in the third person as a sympathetic close friend would. This revealed how they saw themselves in relation to others.
keyPoints: Interview was Kelly's primary assessment technique
Credulous attitude: accept the client's words at face value
Clients may lie, but their words must be respected
Self-characterization sketch: describe oneself as the lead in a play, written by an intimate, sympathetic friend
Reveals how people perceive themselves in relation to others; starting point for fixed role therapy

sections.heading: The Role Construct Repertory Test and The Role of Dichotomies
sections.detailed:
Purpose. Kelly devised the Role Construct Repertory (REP) Test to uncover the constructs we apply to the important people in our lives.

Procedure. The client first lists by name people who have played significant roles in his or her life, such as mother, father, spouse, closest friend, and the most intelligent or most interesting person known. Table 11.2 gives the role title list of 24 roles, including a teacher you liked and one you disliked, your partner, a hard-to-get-along-with employer and a liked one, mother, father, the sibling nearest your age, neighbours, people from high school you liked and disliked, a trip companion you would enjoy and one you would not, someone who seems to dislike you, the person you most want to help, and the most intelligent, successful and interesting people you know.

Sorting in triads. The names are presented three at a time. From each group of three, the client picks the two who are most alike and says how they differ from the third. For example, given most threatening person, successful person and attractive person, the client describes how two are similar in some aspect of behaviour or character and how they differ from the remaining one.

The repertory grid. The information is recorded on a repertory grid (Figure 11.1). For each row the client considers the three people marked with circles and forms a construct about them, such as happy versus sad. The word describing the two similar people (happy) goes in the Emergent Pole column; the opposite word describing the third (sad) goes in the Implicit Pole column. The client then places check marks for anyone else in the grid who shares the emergent pole characteristic, that is, anyone significant who could also be called happy.

The role of dichotomies. The REP Test assumes, following the dichotomy corollary, that people construe events in terms of like versus unlike, similar versus dissimilar. By forcing clients to make repeated judgements about their social relationships, Kelly believed he could uncover their anticipations and expectations. The dichotomies by which we guide our lives reveal the pattern of our personal constructs.

Interpreting the REP Test. Interpretation depends on the skill and training of the psychologist. Kelly did not intend it to be a standardised, objective self-report inventory; he designed it to assess constructs as a necessary stage in psychotherapy, getting clients to reveal the constructs by which they organise their world. Computer programs have since been developed to analyse individual grids more objectively (Grice, 2002). Research later confirmed that the test's validity depends heavily on the interpreter's skill.
sections.simple: In the REP Test, the client lists important people in his or her life, then looks at them three at a time and says how two are alike and differ from the third. This produces constructs like happy versus sad, recorded on a repertory grid with emergent and implicit poles. The test reveals a person's key dichotomies, but interpretation depends on the psychologist's skill.
keyPoints: REP Test uncovers constructs applied to significant people
Client lists people filling 24 role titles (Table 11.2)
Triads: pick two alike and say how they differ from the third
Repertory grid: emergent pole (shared by two), implicit pole (opposite), check marks for others sharing the emergent pole
Assumes dichotomous construing; repeated judgements reveal anticipations
Not standardised; interpretation depends on psychologist's skill; computer analyses now exist (Grice)

sections.heading: Fixed Role Therapy
sections.detailed:
Aim. After assessing a client's construct system, Kelly tried to change undesirable or ineffective constructs through a psychotherapy he called fixed role therapy. To help clients form new constructs and drop old ones, he had them write a self-characterization sketch describing themselves as the lead character in a play.

Playing a role. The therapist then writes a fixed role sketch containing constructs that differ from the client's negative self-perceptions revealed in the self-characterization sketch. The client is told the sketch is about a fictitious character and is asked to act out that character, first in the therapist's office and later in everyday life. Through role-playing, the client is expected to project personal needs and values onto the fictitious character. The therapist expects the client to discover that the new constructs anticipate events better than the old ones; once the client realises this, he or she can incorporate the new constructs into the overall system and function more satisfyingly and effectively. The margin definition: a technique in which the client acts out constructs suited to a fictitious person, showing how new constructs can be more effective than the old.

Origin. Kelly got the idea from watching a friend who began to live the role he played in a college play; offstage, the friend's behaviour gradually came to resemble the character's. So the goal of fixed role therapy is first to play a role and then to come to live it.

Sample case: Roy Taylor. From interviews, a self-characterization sketch and REP Test results, a therapist concluded that this male client was overly preoccupied with finding a female companion, and his efforts were harming his other relationships. He found it hard to be open and assertive because his construct system treated assertiveness and extraversion as negative traits. Yet he was convinced his opinions were right and everyone else's wrong, and at work he felt isolated, believing he belonged to a higher social class than his colleagues. The therapist's fixed role sketch did not mention his wish for an intimate relationship. Instead, using his skill at tennis as a framework, it encouraged him, through the fictitious character, to be more curious about and tolerant of different kinds of people and their views (Winter, 1992). The sketch portrays a man who plays to the best of his ability, works hard and has fun, learns from disappointments and looks forward, anticipates other players' moves, tries to see the world through others' eyes, and respects others' right to disagree.

Role of the therapist. The therapist reviewed the sketch with the client and asked whether the character seemed like someone the client might want to know. The client agreed to try behaving like the character in the office and was asked to act, think and talk like him for the next two weeks. Behavioural changes from fixed role therapy are reported to last far beyond the two-week period.

Evidence. Positive individual case reports must be balanced against the scarcity of controlled research on the technique. One of the few studies found that fixed role therapy reduced social anxiety in a small sample of clients in Japan (Abe, Imai, and Nedate, 2011).
sections.simple: In fixed role therapy, the therapist writes a sketch of a fictitious character whose constructs differ from the client's negative self-view. The client acts out this character in therapy and daily life for about two weeks, discovering that the new constructs work better. Kelly got the idea from a friend who started living his stage role; evidence is mostly case reports plus one small Japanese study.
keyPoints: Therapy to replace ineffective constructs, starting from the self-characterization sketch
Therapist writes a fixed role sketch of a fictitious character with new constructs
Client acts out the role in the office, then in daily life (about two weeks)
Origin: a friend who came to live his college-play role; goal is to play a role, then live it
Roy Taylor case: tennis-based sketch promoting curiosity and tolerance (Winter, 1992)
Little controlled research; Abe, Imai and Nedate (2011) found reduced social anxiety in Japan

sections.heading: Research on Kelly's Theory: Stability of Constructs over Time
sections.detailed:
Stability. REP Test studies show that a person's constructs stay stable over time. In one study subjects took the test twice, naming different people as role figures each time. Even though the role figures changed, the constructs important to the subjects stayed the same. However, research also shows that the validity of the REP Test depends heavily on the skill of the psychologist interpreting the results.

Complexity across the life span. A REP Test study of the complexity of construct systems found that the pattern grows increasingly differentiated and integrated across the life span, and can process more information as it becomes able to function in more abstract terms (Crockett, 1982).

Friendship and similarity of constructs. Another line of research suggested that forming friendships depends on similar personal constructs. Students took the REP Test in their first week of college and again six months later. The similarity in constructs or attitudes among friends had not developed over the six months; it existed before the friendships formed. The researchers concluded that we seek out as friends people whose constructs are already similar to ours (Duck and Spencer, 1972).

Marriage. Among married subjects, spouses whose constructs were more alike reported greater marital happiness than couples whose constructs were less alike (Neimeyer, 1984).

Exam use. These findings are summarised in the chapter's Highlights box: constructs remain stable over time; we choose friends whose constructs are like ours; spouses with similar constructs are happier.
sections.simple: REP Test research shows our constructs stay the same over time, even when we rate different people. Construct systems get more differentiated and integrated as we age. We pick friends whose constructs already match ours, and couples with similar constructs are happier.
keyPoints: Constructs are stable over time even when different role figures are used
REP Test validity depends heavily on the interpreter's skill
Construct systems become more differentiated, integrated and abstract over the life span (Crockett, 1982)
Friends' construct similarity existed before friendship formed (Duck & Spencer, 1972)
Spouses with similar constructs report happier marriages (Neimeyer, 1984)

sections.heading: Effects of Emotional State
sections.detailed:
Personal characteristics and construing others. Research has shown a correspondence between a person's own characteristics and the way he or she construes others. Among student nurses, those identified as highly anxious tended to use anxious versus non-anxious as a construct for judging others, while those judged by peers as friendly tended to view others in terms of friendly versus unfriendly (Sechrest, 1968).

Clinical groups. The REP Test has been used with schizophrenics, neurotics, depressives and people with organic brain damage. Compared with normal subjects, schizophrenics were unstable and inconsistent in construing other people, but stable and consistent in construing objects, suggesting their thought disorder applied only to social situations. Their thinking was also marked by paranoid delusions and irrational links between constructs (for example, Bannister, Fransella, and Agnew, 1971; Bannister and Salmon, 1966; Winter, 1992).

Repeat versus first-time psychiatric patients. A study using a modified REP Test compared repeat psychiatric inpatients with first-time patients. Repeat patients construed their social network as small, limited to a few people they believed they could depend on; first-time patients construed theirs as significantly larger (Smith, Stefan, Kovaleski, and Johnson, 1991).

Offenders. REP Test research with juvenile and adult offenders found that delinquents tended to identify with action-oriented television heroes rather than real adults. Newly released prisoners showed poor self-esteem and lowered aspirations. Rapists felt inadequate, immature and preoccupied with personal failure (Needs, 1988).
sections.simple: How we judge others reflects our own traits: anxious nurses rated people as anxious or not, friendly ones as friendly or not. Schizophrenics construed objects consistently but people inconsistently. Repeat psychiatric patients saw their social networks as small, and delinquents identified with TV action heroes rather than real adults.
keyPoints: Anxious nurses used anxious vs non-anxious; friendly nurses used friendly vs unfriendly (Sechrest, 1968)
REP Test used with schizophrenics, neurotics, depressives, brain-damaged patients
Schizophrenics: inconsistent construing of people, stable construing of objects; paranoid delusions, irrational links (Bannister and colleagues)
Repeat psychiatric patients construed smaller social networks than first-timers (Smith et al., 1991)
Delinquents identified with TV action heroes; released prisoners had low self-esteem; rapists felt inadequate (Needs, 1988)

sections.heading: Real-World Applications and Research on Personal Constructs
sections.detailed:
Real-world applications. The REP Test has been used in market research to identify the criteria consumers use to evaluate products. Industrial-organizational psychologists have applied it to vocational counselling, employee selection, job performance evaluation and evaluation of training programmes (Benjafield, 2008).

Research on personal constructs in nontherapeutic settings. Studies outside therapy have looked at many behaviours that may be influenced by personal constructs.

Reckless driving. A study in Australia found that the degree of drivers' reckless behaviour on the road could be related to the constructs they held (McNally and Bradley, 2014).

Teaching statistics. An American professor teaching in Paris coached beginning statistics students not only to understand statistics but to become enthusiastic about it, by relating the methods to their personal constructs (Clayson, 2013).

Terrorism. A study by British psychologists, described as groundbreaking, examined the personal constructs of convicted Islamic terrorists in India. Those unable to re-construe their future lives in ways not linked to terrorism were the least likely to disengage from future terrorist acts (Canter, Sarangi, and Youngs, 2014). This finding echoes constructive alternativism: the ability to construe alternatives is linked to the capacity for change.
sections.simple: The REP Test is used in market research and in workplace psychology for career counselling, hiring and evaluation. Personal constructs have been linked to reckless driving, used to make statistics students enthusiastic, and studied in terrorists, where those who could not imagine a non-terrorist future were least likely to quit.
keyPoints: REP Test used in market research on consumer criteria
I-O uses: vocational counselling, selection, performance and training evaluation (Benjafield, 2008)
Reckless driving related to drivers' constructs (McNally & Bradley, 2014)
Relating statistics to students' constructs built understanding and enthusiasm (Clayson, 2013)
Terrorists who could not re-construe their futures were least likely to disengage (Canter, Sarangi & Youngs, 2014)

sections.heading: Cognitive Complexity and Cognitive Simplicity
sections.detailed:
Cognitive styles. An outgrowth of Kelly's work concerns cognitive styles: differences in how we perceive or construe the people, objects and situations around us. Research on cognitive styles came from the REP Test and centres on cognitive complexity.

Definitions. Cognitive complexity is the ability to discriminate when applying personal constructs to other people. Highly complex people see variety among people and can easily place a person in many categories. At the other extreme, cognitive simplicity means being less able to perceive differences when judging others; such people tend to place others in only one or two categories. The margin glossary defines both as cognitive styles of construing the environment, marked respectively by the ability or relative inability to perceive differences among people.

Effects on personality and behaviour. People high in cognitive complexity are better at predicting others' behaviour, recognise differences between themselves and others more readily, show more empathy, and handle inconsistent information about others better than cognitively simple people (Crockett, 1982). Studies of college students in the United States and Canada found that complex individuals are lower in anxiety and instability, adjust better to college stress, and tend to show more than the traditional five factors of personality; people lower in complexity show fewer than five factors, suggesting they are less complex emotionally (Bowler, Bowler, and Phillips, 2009; Lester, 2009; Pancer, Hunsberger, Pratt, and Alisat, 2000). Studies of politicians in the United States and England found conservatives high in cognitive simplicity and moderates and liberals higher in complexity (Tetlock, 1983, 1984). Mental health counsellors and therapists with more training and experience showed greater complexity than those with less (Granello, 2010; Owen and Lindley, 2010).

Why complexity is preferred. In Kelly's theory cognitive complexity is the more desirable and useful style. The goal of a construct system is to reduce uncertainty by predicting what people will do, which guides our own behaviour; complex people do this better. So cognitive style is an important dimension of personality.

Changes over time. Complexity increases with age, with adults generally more complex than children. But age is not the whole story; many adults remain cognitively simple. Much depends on the complexity of childhood experiences: complex adults usually had more diverse childhood experiences, and their parents were less authoritarian and more willing to grant autonomy than the parents of cognitively simple adults (Sechrest and Jackson, 1961).

Becoming alike or being alike? In a study of 40 couples, women scored significantly higher in complexity than men, yet partners' complexity scores were highly correlated. The researcher suggested partners may have chosen each other for similar pre-existing complexity, or grown similar by living together; either way they construed their worlds similarly (Adams-Webber, 2001).

Cultural factors. Bicultural Chinese-American students (born in China, at least five years in the United States) scored higher in cognitive complexity than monocultural Anglo-American students (Benet-Martinez, Lee, and Leu, 2006).

Attributional complexity. A variant of cognitive complexity, attributional complexity is the extent to which people prefer complex rather than simple explanations of social behaviour, attributing others' behaviour to complicated, multifaceted, sophisticated causes. People high in it are more sensitive to subtle signs of racism and show more empathy and understanding of others (Foels and Reid, 2010; Reid and Foels, 2010). Business leaders high in attributional complexity manage more effectively than those low in it (Sun and Anderson, 2012).
sections.simple: Cognitively complex people see many differences among people and sort them into many categories; cognitively simple people use only one or two. Complex people predict others better, are more empathic, less anxious and adjust better, and Kelly's theory sees complexity as the better style. Complexity grows with age and diverse childhood experience; attributional complexity means preferring complex explanations of others' behaviour.
keyPoints: Cognitive complexity: ability to discriminate among people; cognitive simplicity: relative inability
Complex people predict others better, are more empathic, handle inconsistency (Crockett, 1982)
Complex students: less anxious, adjust better, more than five personality factors (Bowler et al.; Lester; Pancer et al.)
Conservative politicians simpler, moderates/liberals more complex (Tetlock); experienced therapists more complex (Granello; Owen & Lindley)
Complexity rises with age, diverse childhood experience and less authoritarian parenting (Sechrest & Jackson, 1961); higher in bicultural students (Benet-Martinez et al., 2006)
Attributional complexity: preference for complex explanations; linked to empathy, sensitivity to subtle racism, better management

sections.heading: Reflections on Kelly's Theory
sections.detailed:
Originality. Kelly produced a unique and radical theory that did not derive from or build on others. It arose from his own interpretation, his own construct system, of data from his clinical practice. Its originality parallels its message: we can build the framework for our own lives.

Criticisms.
1. Neglect of emotion. The theory focuses on intellectual and rational functioning to the exclusion of emotional aspects. Kelly's picture of a person rationally constructing present and future, forming and testing hypotheses and making predictions does not match the daily experience of clinical psychologists who see more extreme behaviour; to them Kelly's rational being seems an abstract ideal, not reality. Kelly did not deal explicitly with emotions, though he recognised them as personal constructs formed like any other.
2. Unrepresentative sample. Just as Freud's view came from neurotic, middle-class Viennese patients, Kelly's view was limited mostly to Midwestern young adults defining construct systems to cope with college life.
3. Unanswered questions. Why does one person construe an event one way and another person differently; what process or mechanism accounts for that? And what determines whether a person opts for security or adventure, the safer or the riskier alternative?
4. (From the summary) Omission of familiar concepts such as motivation and emotion.

Continuing support. The theory enjoys a large and growing base of support, though much broader in Europe, Canada and Australia than in the United States. In the mid-1980s the Centre for Personal Construct Psychology was founded in England to train clinicians and promote applications. The International Journal of Personal Construct Psychology and the Journal of Constructivist Psychology began in the late 1980s, and the series Advances in Personal Construct Psychology began in 1990.

Why less popular in the United States. First, many psychologists see it as too different from prevailing ideas; personality psychologists think in terms of motivation, emotion, unconscious forces, drives and needs, none of which appear in Kelly's system. Second, Kelly published few books, articles or case studies, spending most of his time on clinical work and training graduate students. His two major books are scholarly, not aimed at the public or at therapists seeking explanations of passions, loves, hatreds, fears and dreams.

Kelly's own stance and legacy. Kelly recognised the limitations of his work and did not claim a finished theory; just as personal constructs change with experience, he expected the theory to change with research and application. He was honoured by the profession and by former students. The theory is among the most unusual in a century of personality theorising, and adherents apply it in clinical and industrial psychology, anthropology, criminology and urban planning to modify and predict behaviour (Butt, 2008; Walker and Winter, 2007).
sections.simple: Kelly's theory is highly original but criticised for ignoring emotion, relying on rational college students, and leaving open why people construe differently or choose security over adventure. It is more popular in Europe, Canada and Australia than in the US, partly because it is so different and Kelly published little. It is still applied in many fields.
keyPoints: Unique, radical theory derived from Kelly's own construing of clinical data
Criticised for focusing on rationality and excluding emotion (though emotions treated as constructs)
Unrepresentative sample: Midwestern young adult students
Unanswered: why people construe differently; what decides security vs adventure
Support stronger in Europe, Canada, Australia; Centre for PCP (mid-1980s), journals (late 1980s), Advances series (1990)
Less popular in US: too different, few publications, scholarly style; still applied in many fields

terms.definition: Kelly's account of personality in terms of cognitive processes: people interpret behaviour and events and use that understanding to guide their own behaviour and predict others'.
An intellectual hypothesis a person devises and uses to interpret or explain life events; constructs are bipolar, such as tall versus short or honest versus dishonest.
The unique overall pattern of constructs each individual creates to make sense of the world, compared to tinted sunglasses through which events are seen.
The idea that we are not controlled by our constructs but are free to revise or replace them with alternatives as needed.
Kelly's basic proposition that our psychological processes are directed by the ways in which we anticipate events.
Because repeated events share similarities, we can anticipate how we will experience such events in future, though no event is experienced identically twice.
People differ in how they perceive and interpret events, and so form different constructs.
We arrange our constructs into patterns, usually hierarchies, according to their perceived similarities and differences.
A narrower construct contained within a broader one in the construct hierarchy, as intelligent and moral may sit under good.
How well a construct or construct system predicts events; Kelly called it the only valid test of a construct system.
All constructs are bipolar, framed as a pair of mutually exclusive alternatives such as honest versus dishonest.
For each construct we choose the alternative that works best for us, the one allowing us to predict the outcome of events.
Kelly's framing of choice between a low-risk, low-reward option that defines the construct system and a high-risk, high-reward option that extends it.
