Constructs may apply to many situations or people or be limited to a single person or situation.
The spectrum of events to which a construct can be applied; some constructs are relevant to few people or situations, others are broader.
We continually test our constructs against life's experiences and revise or replace those that no longer predict well.
We may modify our constructs as a function of new experiences, depending on their permeability.
The idea that constructs can be revised and extended in light of new experiences; permeable constructs admit new elements into their range of convenience.

We may hold contradictory or inconsistent subordinate constructs within an overall construct system without damaging it.
Although constructs are unique, people in compatible groups or cultures may construe events similarly and so hold similar constructs.
We try to understand how others construe events and predict what they will do, and modify our behaviour accordingly.
A pattern of behaviour that develops from understanding how another person construes events, such as roles with a partner, child or supervisor.
Kelly's stance in interviewing of accepting the client's words at face value as the best way to discover his or her constructs.
A technique for assessing a person's construct system, showing how a person perceives himself or herself in relation to others, written as if by an intimate, sympathetic friend.
Kelly's test to uncover the constructs a person applies to the significant people in his or her life, using triads of role figures.
The diagram on which REP Test information is recorded, with rows of triads, an emergent pole column, an implicit pole column and check marks.
On the repertory grid, the word or phrase describing how two people in a triad are alike (e.g., happy).
On the repertory grid, the opposite word describing the third person in the triad (e.g., sad).
A psychotherapeutic technique in which the client acts out constructs appropriate for a fictitious person, showing how new constructs can be more effective than old ones.
The therapist-written description of a fictitious character whose constructs differ from the client's negative self-perceptions, which the client then enacts.
Differences in how people perceive or construe the persons, objects and situations in their environment.
A cognitive style marked by the ability to perceive differences among people and place them in many categories.
A cognitive style marked by a relative inability to perceive differences among people, placing them in only one or two categories.

studies.title: Fixed role therapy case: Roy Taylor (Winter, 1992)
studies.finding: A tennis-based fixed role sketch encouraging curiosity and tolerance was used with a client preoccupied with finding a partner; changes reportedly lasted beyond the two-week role period.

studies.title: Fixed role therapy and social anxiety (Abe, Imai & Nedate, 2011)
studies.finding: Fixed role therapy reduced social anxiety in a small sample of clients in Japan; one of few controlled studies.

studies.title: Stability of constructs (REP Test retest)
studies.finding: Subjects retested with different role figures still showed the same important constructs, so constructs are stable over time.

studies.title: Validity of the REP Test
studies.finding: The test's validity depends heavily on the skill of the psychologist interpreting it.

studies.title: Construct system complexity over the life span (Crockett, 1982)
studies.finding: Construct systems become increasingly differentiated and integrated with age and process more information as they function more abstractly.

studies.title: Friendship and construct similarity (Duck & Spencer, 1972)
studies.finding: Students tested in week one and six months later: friends' construct similarity predated the friendship, so we choose friends with similar constructs.

studies.title: Marital happiness (Neimeyer, 1984)
studies.finding: Spouses with more similar constructs reported greater marital happiness.

studies.title: Student nurses' construing (Sechrest, 1968)
studies.finding: Highly anxious nurses construed others as anxious vs non-anxious; peer-rated friendly nurses used friendly vs unfriendly.

studies.title: Schizophrenic construing (Bannister et al., 1966, 1971; Winter, 1992)

studies.finding: Repeat patients construed their social networks as small and dependable-few; first-time patients saw significantly larger networks.

studies.title: Offenders (Needs, 1988)

examples.title: Constructs as tinted lenses: a cricket match
examples.text: Two friends watch the same India match. One sees a captain's bold declaration as smart leadership; the other sees it as reckless. Same event, different constructs (bold vs timid, smart vs reckless): the individuality corollary in action.

examples.title: Security vs adventure: choosing a college elective
examples.text: A student can pick the familiar commerce elective she already half-knows, or a new data-science elective with a strict professor. The first is predictable (defines her construct system); the second is risky but could extend it.

examples.title: Permeable vs impermeable constructs
examples.text: Someone who thinks 'people from my rival town are rude' but changes the view after meeting kind people from there has a permeable construct. Someone who keeps the belief no matter what has an impermeable one.

examples.title: Sociality corollary: auto-rickshaw traffic
examples.text: Crossing a busy road, you predict that the auto driver will slow down when you raise your hand, and he predicts you will wait if he honks. Each construes the other's constructs and adjusts.

examples.title: Fixed role therapy: the shy student
examples.text: A shy student who sees himself as boring is given a sketch of a curious character who asks people questions. After two weeks of acting the part, he finds conversations go better and starts to adopt the new constructs.

practice.q: Define a construct. Why must constructs be dichotomous?
practice.answer: A construct is an intellectual hypothesis a person devises to interpret, explain and predict life events. By the dichotomy corollary every construct is bipolar (e.g., honest versus dishonest), because a quality can only be predicted in contrast to its opposite; if everyone were honest, the construct honesty would distinguish and predict nothing.

practice.q: What is constructive alternativism?
practice.answer: Constructive alternativism is Kelly's idea that we are not controlled by our constructs but are free to revise or replace them with alternatives as situations change. Because there is always another way to construe events, we can cope with new situations; if constructs were fixed by childhood, we could not adapt.

practice.q: What is a construct's range of convenience? Illustrate with the construct cheerful versus sad.
practice.answer: The range of convenience is the spectrum of events to which a construct can be applied; some constructs are broad, others narrow, and the range is a personal choice. One person may apply cheerful versus sad to people only, another also to music, places or weather. Kelly held that what a construct excludes matters as much as what it includes.

practice.q: What mechanism did Kelly propose to explain changes in a construct's range of convenience?
practice.answer: Permeability (modulation corollary). A permeable construct lets new elements enter its range of convenience, so it can be revised and extended by new experiences. An impermeable construct, such as a prejudiced belief, cannot change however much contrary experience a person has.

practice.q: What is a self-characterization sketch and how is it used in therapy?
practice.answer: It is a sketch the client writes about himself or herself, as the main character in a play, as an intimate and sympathetic friend might write it. It reveals how the person perceives himself or herself in relation to others, and in fixed role therapy it shows the negative self-perceptions that the therapist's fixed role sketch is designed to replace.

practice.q: How do people high in attributional complexity view others' behaviour?
practice.answer: They prefer complex rather than simple explanations, attributing others' behaviour to multifaceted, sophisticated causes. Research links high attributional complexity to greater sensitivity to subtle racism, more empathy and understanding (Foels and Reid, 2010), and more effective management in business leaders (Sun and Anderson, 2012).

practice.q: What did Kelly mean by saying that we all function like scientists? How does his approach differ from other approaches to personality?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly's personal construct theory rests on the image of the person as a scientist, an idea he drew from his clinical work with rational student clients.

People as scientists. Scientists form theories and hypotheses, test them against reality and keep, revise or reject them according to the results. Kelly argued that everyone does the same in daily life. We observe events, interpret them in our own way and build personal constructs, hypotheses we use to predict and control what happens. We act on these constructs and judge them by how well they predict; the student who flatters an authoritarian professor keeps the construct if the grade improves and drops it if not. Kelly criticised psychologists for treating themselves as rational while treating their subjects as emotional or driven by unconscious forces; psychologists are not superior beings, since both predict and control events rationally.

Differences from other approaches. Kelly's system omits the unconscious, ego, needs, drives, stimuli and responses, reinforcement, and even motivation and emotion. Like Maslow he opposed behaviourism (people as passive responders to stimuli) and psychoanalysis (people as passive responders to unconscious forces); for Kelly people propel themselves. Interpretation of events matters more than the events themselves, and personality is an ongoing process directed by anticipation of the future rather than by the past.

Conclusion. Kelly's scientist model makes personality a matter of conscious, rational construing, setting his theory apart from every other approach in the book.

practice.q: Explain the relationship between Kelly's theory and modern cognitive psychology, and how his clients may have influenced his theory.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly's theory is described as cognitive, but its links with the cognitive movement are weak, and its cognitive emphasis may reflect the kind of clients he treated.

Relationship with cognitive psychology. The cognitive movement began around 1960 and dominates experimental psychology, yet it did not embrace Kelly's work because his theory does not match its subject matter and methods. Kelly was a clinician concerned with the conscious constructs by which people arrange their lives. Cognitive psychologists study both cognitive variables and overt behaviour, mainly in experimental settings, and look beyond personality to behaviour and learning in social situations. Kelly's theory had little influence on cognitive psychology and is at best a precursor; the two share the term cognitive and an interest in conscious activity but little else. It is not mainstream, yet remains useful for studying personality.

Influence of clients. At Fort Hays during the Depression Kelly counselled students referred by teachers, not hospitalised psychotics or severely troubled neurotics. These clients could discuss problems rationally and in intellectual terms, carrying the classroom's analytical attitude into counselling. The chapter suggests that if he had worked with schizophrenics in an institution, his theory might not have relied so heavily on cognitive information-processing abilities. His sample is also criticised as unrepresentative, limited largely to Midwestern young adults.

Conclusion. Kelly's cognitive theory is a clinical, not experimental, tradition, shaped by rational student clients.

practice.q: Explain the choice corollary. How do we choose between the two alternatives offered by a construct?
practice.answer:
Introduction. The choice corollary expresses Kelly's belief in freedom of choice. Because every construct has two poles (dichotomy corollary), we must choose between them in every situation.

Basis of choice. We choose the alternative that works best for us, the one that lets us anticipate or predict outcomes. Our choices are made according to how well they help prediction, not necessarily according to what is best for us, since each of us wants to predict the future with the highest possible certainty.

Security versus adventure. Kelly described our latitude as a choice between security and adventure. An easy course similar to one already taken, with a lenient but dull professor, is the secure option: low risk, low reward and high predictive efficiency. A course in an unfamiliar, interesting subject with a tough new professor is adventurous: high risk, high potential reward, lower predictive efficiency. The secure choice repeats past experience and so defines and limits the construct system; the adventurous choice extends it to new experiences.

Application. This explains persistent unrewarding behaviour: people who stay aggressive despite rebuffs choose aggression because they know what to expect, while friendliness, rarely tried, is uncertain.

Conclusion. Choice is guided by predictability. Critics note Kelly did not explain what decides whether a person opts for security or adventure.

practice.q: Explain how the individuality corollary differs from the organization corollary.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Both corollaries explain why people differ, but at different levels: the content of constructs versus their arrangement.

Individuality corollary. This corollary introduced individual differences into Kelly's theory. People differ in how they perceive and interpret an event, so they form different constructs. Constructs do not so much mirror objective reality as express the unique interpretation each person places on it, like tinted lenses colouring the same scene differently.

Organization corollary. This corollary deals with relationships among constructs. We arrange constructs into patterns according to their perceived similarities and differences, usually as a hierarchy in which some constructs are subordinate to others; for example good may include intelligent and moral, so a person seen as good is expected to be intelligent and moral. Relationships among constructs are more enduring than specific constructs but can change: someone insulted by a more intelligent person might move intelligent under bad. The only valid test of the system is predictive efficiency.

The difference. Individuality concerns which constructs people form; organization concerns how constructs are structured. Even people with similar constructs can differ if they organise them in different patterns.

Conclusion. Together the two corollaries explain differences in both what people think and how their thinking is structured.

practice.q: How is it possible to hold incompatible constructs? Explain with reference to the fragmentation corollary.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly's fragmentation corollary states that we may hold contradictory or inconsistent subordinate constructs within an overall construct system.

Why inconsistency arises. The construct system changes as we evaluate new experiences, but new constructs do not necessarily derive from old ones. A new construct may be consistent with an old one in one situation but become inconsistent when the situation changes.

Example. A man meets a woman in a psychology class; she shares his major and interests, so she fits the friend pole of his friend versus enemy construct. The next day at a political rally she loudly expresses conservative views opposed to his liberal ones, and now she fits the enemy pole. In one situation she is a friend, in another an enemy.

How we tolerate it. The inconsistency lies at the subordinate level. His broader superordinate construct, that liberals are friends and conservatives are enemies, is not disturbed. According to Kelly, confining contradictions to situation-specific subordinate constructs lets us tolerate them without damaging the overall system. The chapter's illustration of people who are friends over a board game but adversaries in a political debate makes the same point.

Conclusion. Hierarchical organisation makes fragmentation possible: lower-level contradictions coexist with higher-level consistency.

practice.q: Why is it important to construe the constructs of other people? Discuss the sociality and commonality corollaries.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly's last two corollaries deal with the social side of construing.

Commonality corollary. Although constructs are unique, people also construe events similarly. If several people construe an experience alike, their cognitive processes are similar. People sharing cultural norms and ideals have common anticipations and expectations of one another, so they may resemble each other in behaviour despite different life events.

Sociality corollary. Similar construing alone does not create positive relationships. One person must also construe the other's constructs, understanding how the other thinks in order to anticipate how that person will predict events. We do this routinely: drivers stake their lives on predicting that others will stop at red lights and go on green. Only when we can predict what drivers, friends, bosses or teachers will do can we adjust to them, while they adjust to us.

Roles. Each person plays roles with others, with a partner, a child, a supervisor. Each role is a behaviour pattern growing out of understanding how the other construes events; we fit ourselves into the other person's constructs.

Importance. Construing others' constructs enables prediction, coordination, relationships and appropriate roles.

Conclusion. Commonality explains shared outlooks; sociality explains how we actually relate to others by understanding their construing.

practice.q: What is Kelly's position on free will versus determinism and other questions about human nature?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly offers an optimistic, even flattering, image of human nature, treating people as rational beings who construct frameworks for viewing the world.

Free will versus determinism. Kelly grants free will: we choose the direction of our lives and can change by revising old constructs and forming new ones. He rejected determinism; past events do not determine present behaviour. We are not prisoners of toilet training, early sexual experiences or parental rejection, nor bound by instincts or unconscious forces. We are authors, not victims, of our destiny.

Other issues. Motivation: no drives or needs are required, as we are motivated by being alive. Past versus future: our direction is toward the future because constructs anticipate events. Nature versus nurture: heredity is not discussed, but we are not wholly shaped by environment, since it is our rational interpretation of events, not the events themselves, that forms personality. Goal: none is posited, but we may infer it is a construct system that predicts events. Uniqueness versus universality: moderate, balancing the commonality and individuality corollaries.

Conclusion. Kelly's view is free-willed, future-oriented, rational and optimistic, consistent with constructive alternativism.

practice.q: Describe the Role Construct Repertory Test and how it works with clients.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly devised the Role Construct Repertory (REP) Test to uncover the constructs people apply to the significant people in their lives.

Procedure. The client lists by name people who fill important roles, from a 24-item role title list (Table 11.2): liked and disliked teachers, partner, liked and difficult employers, mother, father, nearest-age siblings, neighbours, high-school peers, the most intelligent, successful and interesting people known, and so on. The names are presented three at a time. From each triad the client chooses the two most alike and states how they differ from the third.

The repertory grid. Results go on a repertory grid. For each row the client considers the three circled people and forms a construct, such as happy versus sad. The word for the similar pair goes in the Emergent Pole column, the opposite word for the third person in the Implicit Pole column, and the client ticks anyone else in the grid who shares the emergent pole.

Rationale and interpretation. Based on the dichotomy corollary, the test assumes construing in terms of like versus unlike; repeated judgements reveal the client's anticipations and pattern of constructs. Kelly saw it as a stage in therapy, not a standardised inventory, so interpretation depends on the psychologist's skill, although computer programs now analyse grids more objectively (Grice, 2002).

Conclusion. The REP Test turns Kelly's dichotomy corollary into a practical clinical tool and has also been used in research and industry.

practice.q: What is fixed role therapy? How does it relate to role-playing?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Fixed role therapy is Kelly's technique for replacing undesirable or ineffective constructs with more useful ones.

Procedure. The client first writes a self-characterization sketch. The therapist then writes a fixed role sketch whose constructs differ from the client's negative self-perceptions. The client is told it describes a fictitious character and acts out that character first in the therapist's office, then in everyday life, typically for two weeks.

Role-playing. Through role-playing the client projects personal needs and values onto the character and discovers that the new constructs anticipate events better than the old ones. The client can then incorporate them into the construct system and function more effectively. Kelly got the idea from a friend who began to live the role he played in a college play; the aim is to play a role first and then come to live it.

Example. Roy Taylor, preoccupied with finding a partner and convinced others were wrong, received a tennis-based sketch that encouraged curiosity about and tolerance of different people, without mentioning romance (Winter, 1992). Changes are reported to last beyond the two weeks.

Evidence. Controlled research is scarce; one study found reduced social anxiety in a small Japanese sample (Abe, Imai and Nedate, 2011).

Conclusion. Fixed role therapy applies constructive alternativism: trying out alternative constructs through role enactment.

practice.q: How do people high in cognitive complexity differ from those high in cognitive simplicity?
practice.answer:
Introduction. Cognitive complexity research grew out of the REP Test and concerns cognitive styles, differences in how we construe people and situations.

Definitions. Cognitive complexity is the ability to discriminate when applying constructs to others; complex people see variety and place others in many categories. Cognitive simplicity is relative inability to perceive differences; simple people use only one or two categories.

Differences. Complex people predict others' behaviour better, recognise differences between themselves and others, show more empathy and handle inconsistent information better (Crockett, 1982). North American students high in complexity are lower in anxiety and instability, adjust better to college stress and show more than the five traditional personality factors, while less complex people show fewer, suggesting less emotional complexity. Conservative politicians were high in simplicity and moderates and liberals higher in complexity (Tetlock). More trained and experienced therapists are more complex (Granello; Owen and Lindley).

Origins. Complexity rises with age, but many adults stay simple; complex adults had more diverse childhoods and less authoritarian, autonomy-granting parents (Sechrest and Jackson, 1961). Bicultural students score higher (Benet-Martinez et al., 2006).

Conclusion. In Kelly's terms, complexity is the more desirable style because it better reduces uncertainty by predicting others, making cognitive style an important personality dimension.

practice.q: Explain Kelly's fundamental postulate and its eleven corollaries.
practice.answer:
Introduction. George Kelly presented personal construct theory in a scientific format: a fundamental postulate and 11 corollaries. The theory rests on the view that people act like scientists, forming constructs (bipolar intellectual hypotheses) to interpret and predict events.

The fundamental postulate. Our psychological processes are directed by the ways we anticipate events. "Processes" shows that personality is continually flowing rather than fixed; "anticipate" shows that constructs are tools for predicting the consequences of our actions.

1. Construction corollary. No event is experienced exactly the same way twice, since mood and intervening experiences change, yet recurring themes appear. Because repeated events are similar, we can anticipate future ones; constructs are built from these recurring themes (rewatching a film's car chases).

2. Individuality corollary. People interpret the same event differently and so form different constructs. Constructs reflect personal interpretation more than objective reality.

3. Organization corollary. We arrange constructs in patterns, usually hierarchies, according to their similarities and differences: good may include intelligent and moral. Relationships among constructs are fairly enduring but can change, and the only valid test of the system is predictive efficiency.

4. Dichotomy corollary. All constructs are bipolar. Honest only means something in contrast to dishonest; a single pole would predict nothing.

5. Choice corollary. We choose the pole that best lets us predict outcomes. This is a choice between security (low risk, high predictive efficiency, defining the system) and adventure (high risk, high reward, extending the system). It explains why people persist in predictable but unrewarding behaviour such as aggression.

6. Range corollary. Constructs have a range of convenience: tall versus short fits trees and players but not pizza. The range is a personal choice, and knowing what a construct excludes matters as much as what it includes.

7. Experience corollary. We continually test constructs against new experiences and revise poor predictors; constructs that served at 16 may be useless at 40.

8. Modulation corollary. Our ability to modify constructs depends on their permeability. Permeable constructs admit new elements into their range; impermeable ones, like a bigot's belief about an ethnic group's intelligence, resist all evidence and block learning.

9. Fragmentation corollary. We may hold inconsistent subordinate constructs, as when a classmate is a friend in class but an enemy at a political rally, while the superordinate construct (liberals friends, conservatives enemies) stays intact.

10. Commonality corollary. People in the same culture construe many experiences alike, which shows similar cognitive processes and produces resemblances in behaviour despite different life events.

11. Sociality corollary. Good relationships require construing others' constructs. We predict drivers, friends and bosses and adjust to them, and our roles grow from understanding how others construe events.

Integration. The corollaries form a system: dichotomy makes choice necessary; organization and fragmentation describe structure; experience and modulation explain change, supporting constructive alternativism; individuality and commonality give Kelly's moderate stance on uniqueness; sociality extends the theory to relationships.

Conclusion. The postulate and corollaries portray personality as an active, future-oriented, rational process of anticipating events. They underpin Kelly's optimism and free will, the REP Test and fixed role therapy, though critics argue they neglect emotion and leave open why people construe differently or choose security over adventure.

practice.q: Describe the assessment techniques used in Kelly's theory and his method of fixed role therapy.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly assessed personality by uncovering a person's construct system and then tried to change ineffective constructs. Because he saw people as rational and aware of their constructs, his methods rely on direct report.

The interview. The interview was his primary technique. He advised that if you want to know what is in a person's mind, ask, since the person may tell you. With a credulous attitude he accepted clients' words at face value as the best route to their constructs. He knew clients might lie or distort, but held that what they said must be respected even if not fully believed.

Self-characterization sketch. Clients wrote a sketch of themselves, using their own name, as the main character in a play, written as by an intimate, sympathetic friend who knew them better than anyone could. It shows how a person perceives himself or herself in relation to others.

The Role Construct Repertory (REP) Test. Designed to uncover constructs applied to significant people, the test asks the client to name people filling 24 role titles (liked and disliked teachers, partner, parents, siblings, employers, neighbours, high-school peers, the most intelligent, successful and interesting people known). Names are presented in triads; the client picks two alike and states how they differ from the third. On the repertory grid, the shared quality goes in the Emergent Pole column (e.g., happy), its opposite in the Implicit Pole column (sad), and others sharing the emergent pole are ticked. Based on the dichotomy corollary, repeated like-versus-unlike judgements reveal the client's anticipations and pattern of constructs. Kelly intended the test as a stage in therapy, not a standardised inventory, so interpretation depends on the psychologist's skill; computer programs now permit more objective analysis (Grice, 2002). Research shows constructs measured this way remain stable over time.

Fixed role therapy. After assessment, the therapist writes a fixed role sketch whose constructs differ from the negative self-perceptions in the self-characterization. The client is told the sketch is of a fictitious character and acts it out in the office and then in daily life, typically for two weeks. Through role-playing, the client projects needs and values onto the character and discovers that the new constructs predict events better, then incorporates them. Kelly derived the method from a friend who began to live his college-play role; the goal is to play a role and then live it.

Case of Roy Taylor. Assessment showed a man preoccupied with finding a partner, viewing assertiveness and extraversion as negative, sure that others were wrong and feeling socially superior at work. The sketch ignored romance and used his tennis skills as a framework, portraying a character who plays his best, learns from setbacks, anticipates others' moves, sees through others' eyes and tolerates disagreement (Winter, 1992). The therapist checked that the client would like to know such a person; changes are reported to outlast the two weeks.

Evaluation. Controlled evidence is limited, though Abe, Imai and Nedate (2011) found reduced social anxiety in a small Japanese sample. The REP Test has also been applied in market research and industrial-organizational psychology.

Conclusion. Kelly's assessment methods follow from his trust in people's rational self-knowledge, and fixed role therapy applies constructive alternativism by letting clients try alternative constructs until they work better than the old ones.

practice.q: Discuss the research on Kelly's theory, including cognitive complexity and cognitive simplicity.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Most research on Kelly's theory uses the REP Test. It covers stability of constructs, links between personal characteristics and construing, clinical and offender groups, applications, and the cognitive styles of complexity and simplicity.

Stability and relationships. Subjects retested with different role figures kept the same important constructs, so constructs are stable over time, though the test's validity depends on the interpreter's skill. Construct systems become more differentiated, integrated and abstract across the life span (Crockett, 1982). Students tested in their first week and six months later showed that friends' construct similarity existed before the friendship, so we choose friends with similar constructs (Duck and Spencer, 1972). Spouses with similar constructs report happier marriages (Neimeyer, 1984).

Emotional state and clinical groups. Anxious student nurses construed others as anxious versus non-anxious, and friendly ones as friendly versus unfriendly (Sechrest, 1968). Schizophrenics construed people inconsistently but objects consistently, suggesting a socially specific thought disorder with paranoid delusions and irrational links between constructs (Bannister and colleagues; Winter). Repeat psychiatric patients saw small social networks compared with first-time patients (Smith et al., 1991). Delinquents identified with TV action heroes, released prisoners had low self-esteem and aspirations, and rapists felt inadequate and immature (Needs, 1988).

Applications. The REP Test is used in market research and for vocational counselling, selection, performance and training evaluation (Benjafield, 2008). Constructs relate to reckless driving (McNally and Bradley, 2014), helped make statistics engaging (Clayson, 2013), and convicted terrorists in India unable to re-construe their futures were least likely to disengage (Canter, Sarangi and Youngs, 2014).

Cognitive complexity and simplicity. Cognitive complexity is the ability to discriminate among people when applying constructs; cognitive simplicity is relative inability to do so, placing people in one or two categories. Complex people predict others better, recognise self-other differences, are more empathic and handle inconsistent information better (Crockett, 1982). Complex North American students are less anxious and unstable, adjust better to college and show more than five personality factors (Bowler et al.; Lester; Pancer et al.). Conservative politicians are simpler, moderates and liberals more complex (Tetlock). Experienced therapists are more complex (Granello; Owen and Lindley). Complexity grows with age but depends on diverse childhood experience and less authoritarian, autonomy-granting parents (Sechrest and Jackson, 1961). Partners' complexity is highly correlated, though women scored higher (Adams-Webber, 2001), and bicultural Chinese-American students are more complex than monocultural Anglo-Americans (Benet-Martinez, Lee and Leu, 2006). Kelly's theory treats complexity as more desirable because it better reduces uncertainty.

Attributional complexity. This variant is the preference for complex explanations of social behaviour. It is linked to sensitivity to subtle racism, empathy (Foels and Reid, 2010) and more effective business leadership (Sun and Anderson, 2012).

Conclusion. Research supports the stability and social importance of constructs and shows cognitive style to be a meaningful dimension of personality, though fixed role therapy itself has little controlled research and REP Test interpretation depends on skill.

practice.q: Critically evaluate Kelly's personal construct theory.
practice.answer:
Introduction. Kelly's personal construct theory is among the most unusual in a century of personality theorising. It views people as scientists who construct, test and revise bipolar hypotheses about the world.

Contributions. First, originality: the theory did not build on others but grew from Kelly's own construing of his clinical data, and its message is that we can build the framework of our own lives. Second, a coherent formal structure: a fundamental postulate (processes directed by anticipation) and 11 corollaries covering how constructs are formed, organised, chosen, applied, tested, modified and shared. Third, an optimistic image of human nature: rational beings with free will, oriented to the future, not prisoners of childhood, instincts or the unconscious, with constructive alternativism always leaving room for change. Fourth, practical tools: the interview with a credulous attitude, the self-characterization sketch, the REP Test and fixed role therapy. Fifth, research and applications: REP Test studies show stable constructs, friends and spouses with similar constructs, and distinct construing in schizophrenics and offenders; cognitive complexity research links complexity to prediction, empathy, lower anxiety and adjustment. The theory is applied in market research, industrial-organizational psychology, clinical psychology, anthropology, criminology and urban planning. It has strong support in Europe, Canada and Australia, with the Centre for Personal Construct Psychology (mid-1980s), dedicated journals (late 1980s) and the Advances series (1990).

Criticisms. First, overemphasis on rationality: it focuses on intellectual functioning to the exclusion of emotion. Clinicians who see extreme behaviour regard Kelly's rational being as an abstract ideal; Kelly treated emotions only as constructs. Second, omission of familiar concepts such as motivation, emotion, unconscious forces, drives and needs, which is one reason US psychologists find it too different. Third, an unrepresentative sample: like Freud's Viennese neurotics, Kelly's clients were mostly Midwestern young adults coping with college, and the chapter suggests work with schizophrenics might have produced a less cognitive theory. Fourth, unanswered questions: why do people construe the same event differently, and what decides whether a person chooses security or adventure? Fifth, limited evidence and dissemination: fixed role therapy has little controlled research (one small Japanese study found reduced social anxiety), REP Test validity depends on the interpreter, and Kelly published few books, articles or case studies, in a scholarly style unsuited to general readers. The theory also had little influence on the cognitive movement.

Kelly's own stance. Kelly did not claim a finished theory and expected it to change with research, just as personal constructs change with experience.

Conclusion. Kelly's theory is original, optimistic and practically fruitful, especially through the REP Test and cognitive complexity research. Its neglect of emotion, narrow sample and unanswered questions limit it as a complete account of personality, but it remains influential, particularly outside the United States.

assessment.explain: Kelly organised his theory into a fundamental postulate and 11 corollaries (Table 11.1).

assessment.q: Who did Kelly replace at Ohio State University?
assessment.explain: After the war Kelly joined Ohio State, replacing Carl Rogers.

assessment.q: Which corollary explains how we tolerate inconsistent subordinate constructs?
assessment.explain: The fragmentation corollary allows contradictory subordinate constructs within an intact system.

assessment.q: The mechanism Kelly proposed for changes in a construct's range of convenience is:
assessment.explain: Permeable constructs admit new elements into their range of convenience (modulation corollary).

assessment.q: Choosing the secure alternative tends to:
options: Define and limit the construct system
assessment.explain: Secure choices repeat experiences, defining and limiting the system; adventurous ones extend it.

assessment.q: Which corollary states that we must understand how others think to relate to them?
assessment.explain: The sociality corollary concerns construing others' constructs.

assessment.q: Kelly's position on uniqueness versus universality is best described as:
assessment.explain: Commonality stresses similarity; individuality stresses uniqueness, so his stance is moderate.

assessment.q: The REP Test assumes people construe events in terms of:
assessment.explain: Following the dichotomy corollary, the test assumes like vs unlike construing.

assessment.q: Kelly intended the REP Test to be:
options: A stage in psychotherapy, not a standardised objective inventory
A projective test of the unconscious
assessment.explain: He designed it to induce clients to reveal constructs during therapy.

assessment.q: In the Roy Taylor case, the fixed role sketch was framed around:
assessment.explain: The sketch avoided his romantic concerns and used tennis as the framework.

assessment.q: Repeat psychiatric patients, compared with first-time patients, construed their social networks as:
assessment.explain: Smith et al. (1991) found repeat patients saw small networks of a few dependable people.

assessment.q: Studies by Tetlock found that conservative politicians were high in:
assessment.explain: Conservatives were high in simplicity; moderates and liberals more complex.

assessment.q: In Adams-Webber's (2001) study of 40 couples:
options: Partners' cognitive complexity was highly correlated
assessment.explain: Women scored higher, but partners' scores were highly correlated.

options: Preferring complex explanations of social behaviour
Using only one or two categories
assessment.explain: It is a variant of cognitive complexity concerning explanations of others' behaviour.

assessment.q: Bicultural Chinese-American students, compared with monocultural Anglo-Americans, were:
assessment.explain: Benet-Martinez, Lee and Leu (2006) found bicultural students more complex.

options: He made emotion the core of his theory
He said emotions are unconscious drives
He treated emotions as personal constructs formed like other constructs
assessment.explain: Although he did not deal explicitly with emotion, he recognised emotions as constructs.

assessment.explain: His view was limited largely to Midwestern young adults defining construct systems for college life.
